{% raw %}
`kill`: send a signal to a process.

## Synopsis

<strong>kill</strong> \[<strong>-s</strong> <em>signal</em> \|  <strong>-</strong><em>signal</em><strong>\]</strong> \[<strong>--</strong>\] <em>pid</em>...\
<strong>kill -l</strong>

## Description

<strong>kill</strong> sends a signal to each <em>pid</em>, <strong>SIGTERM</strong> unless another is given. A negative <em>pid</em> is a process group: every process in it gets the signal. Give it after <strong>--</strong> so it isn't read as a signal.

A signal is a name, with or without its <strong>SIG</strong> prefix, in any case (<strong>-KILL</strong>, <strong>-sigint</strong>), or its number (<strong>-9</strong>). The signals mcos knows are <strong>SIGHUP</strong> (1), <strong>SIGINT</strong> (2), <strong>SIGKILL</strong> (9), <strong>SIGPIPE</strong> (13), <strong>SIGTERM</strong> (15) and <strong>SIGCHLD</strong> (17). <strong>SIGKILL</strong> cannot be caught or ignored: the process ends at once and runs none of its code.

## Options

<strong>-s</strong> <em>signal</em>, <strong>-</strong><em>signal</em>
: The signal to send.

<strong>-l</strong>
: Lists the signals, by number.

<strong>--</strong>
: Ends the options: what follows is pids.

## Exit status

0 if every signal was sent; 1 if any failed (no such process, a pid that isn't a number, an unknown signal); 2 with no pid.

## Examples

```text
kill 12
kill -9 12 13
kill -s INT 7
kill -TERM -- -5
```

## See also

<strong>ps</strong>(1), <strong>sh</strong>(1)
